name: Parintintin Tenharim
confidence_why: Betts 1981 and Marçoli 2018 both put stress on the last syllable of the root, and the phrase-initial stress that Gordon 2002 and StressTyp2 took from Pease and Betts 1971 as initial word stress falls on root-final syllables in that paper's own transcribed text, so the placement is final, not initial.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the last syllable of the stem (radical) in nearly all words; the dictionary writes an acute accent only on the minority of items whose stress departs from this rule. The Esboço Gramatical adds (p. 13) that in verb reduplication 'É sempre a última sílaba acentuada que é reduplicada' (it is always the last stressed syllable that is reduplicated), and the pronunciation key refers to 'sílabas não-acentuadas' (unstressed syllables) when describing the allophones of j, so a stressed/unstressed distinction is assumed throughout.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Quase sempre' (almost always): lexical exceptions exist and are marked with the diacritic in the dictionary; no examples are given in the key. The domain is the stem (radical), not the whole word, so unstressed suffixes/enclitics can follow the stressed syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: Betts 1981 describes Parintintin (Kagwahiva) as spoken on the Rio Madeira, the variety the SIL team worked with; Pease & Betts 1971 is titled 'Parintintin: a dialect of Tenharim'. Marcoli 2018 and dos Santos 2024 treat Parintintin/Tenharim/Juma as dialects of one Kawahiva language; dos Santos notes the /h/-deletion facts for the Juma dialect specifically.

audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant FINAL (root-final, right-edge; final stress), not strict: stress on the last syllable of the root = word-final in the default case, penultimate when an unstressed suffix/enclitic (-a 'argumentative', postposition -pe, etc.) follows; stressed suffixes (-u'hu, e'te) take the stress. Cite Betts 1981 p.8 + Marçoli 2018 pp.77,122-123 as deciding sources; keep Pease & Betts 1971 p.10 as the phrase-level source and note that StressTyp2's 'initial' is a misreading of a phrase-stress statement whose phrases were segmented at the stressed syllable.
audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim at Pease & Betts 1971 p.10 §5.1 in the held archive.org text and PDF page image. (2) But the classification it supports ('initial', from StressTyp2/Gordon 2002) rests on a tentative phrase-level statement; the same paper's transcribed text (p.13) shows the 'phrase-initial' stressed syllables are root-final syllables with phrase boundaries drawn inside words (ha/'ko, ne/'piakA, re/'koiV, rero/\"ho, o/'re). (3) Two held primary sources by the same fieldworkers give the word rule explicitly as root-final: Betts 1981 p.8 'Quase sempre o acento ocorre na ultima sílaba do radical' (dictionary marks stress only on exceptions), p.14 reduplication copies 'a última sílaba acentuada'; Pease 1968/2007 p.2 (ndurí, nduví: stress moves to suffix -i), p.18 ('final stressed syllable').
